# SPD-062 — Bash hook: a PATH assignment in force replaces the very program the hook checked

## Brief
The hook reads a line's command words by name (git, spud, python3.14, sqlite3, tee, a wrapper's command) and then lets the shell find them on PATH. A PATH assignment in force on the line is never read, so a member that puts its own directory first runs its own program under a name the hook cleared: `PATH=<dir>:$PATH git status` runs <dir>/git, which can do anything git could, and the same trick serves for spud, python, sqlite3 or any wrapper. This is the same class as SPD-044 (config injected by variable) and SPD-046 (config that names a program), one level up: the program itself, not what git runs. The fix is the shape SPD-046 used for GIT_PAGER and friends: PATH (and zsh's path array, and anything that prepends to it, plus GIT_EXEC_PATH, already covered) in force by prefix assignment, export or the env wrapper is refused for a member whenever the line dispatches on a command name, with its own reason. Out of SPD-047's scope, which is aliases and config files git reads.

Evidence: Probed for SPD-047 (git 2.54.0, scratchpad only): `PATH=<dir>:$PATH git foo` ran <dir>/git-foo, so a directory first on PATH is honoured for the git-* dispatch and, by the same mechanism, for git itself. analyse_command on the new tree gives no finding at all for the assignment: 'PATH=/tmp/x:$PATH git status', 'PATH=/tmp/x git status', 'export PATH=/tmp/x; git status' and 'env PATH=/tmp/x git status' each yield kinds ['git'] and findings [('git', ('status', None))] -- the hook sees an allowed read verb and says nothing, while the shell would run /tmp/x/git. 'PATH=/tmp/x ls' yields kind 'other' with no finding. bin/spud_ledger.py: is_git_program_var/GIT_PROGRAM_ENV_VARS (about line 5740) is where GIT_EXEC_PATH is already refused; nothing reads PATH.

## Size, persona and model decision
Cluster B of Eric's batch of 2026-09-15: SPD-062, SPD-055 and SPD-051, the second engineer on opus, no children, after cluster A lands on the batch branch. All three are the same class: the program the shell runs is not the program the hook checked by name.
